verdicts.quote: contentLength is read as unsigned int (0 to 4GB), but only checked if it is less than Integer.MAX_VALUE. No upper bound validation or rate limiting. A contentLength of 2GB would be allocated on line 88: byte[] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength].
verdicts.why: F04 is about exactly the mechanism in D1: an attacker-controlled length field (contentLength) read from the wire directly sizes a heap buffer (new byte[(int)contentLength]) that is allocated up front, with no check that the stream actually holds that many bytes -- only a comparison against Integer.MAX_VALUE. The exploit it describes (send a huge declared length with no payload behind it, force a multi-GB allocation) is the length-decides-buffer-size-before-payload-exists mechanism, not a different one. F03/F06 are neighbours but they are about unbounded element counts in HashMap/List growth, which is a different mechanism.

verdicts.quote: readTable and readArray recursively call readFieldValue, which can parse nested tables (case 'F') and arrays (case 'A'). No recursion depth limit is enforced.
verdicts.why: F10 states the mutual-recursion cycle by name (readTable/readArray -> readFieldValue -> readTable/readArray) and identifies the missing depth counter as what makes it exploitable, with nesting in the attacker-supplied message controlling the depth and the impact being stack overflow. That is precisely D2's mechanism.
